q: 1. Estimate is
options: the actual cost of construction of a structure
The probable cost arrived at before commencement of the structure
a random guess of the cost of the structure
explain: An estimate is a technically calculated probable cost worked out from drawings, specifications, and rates before construction begins — it is not the final actual cost.

q: 2. Which of the following is the most correct estimate?
explain: A detailed estimate works out quantities of every item separately and multiplies by its rate, giving the closest approximation to actual cost among all estimate types.

q: 3. A document containing detailed description of all items of work (but their quantities are not mentioned) together with their current rates is called
explain: A Schedule of Rates lists standard items of work with their current unit rates, without specifying quantities for a particular project.

q: 4. Working out the exact quantities of various items of work is known as
explain: Quantity surveying is the process of measuring and calculating the exact quantities of materials and work items from drawings.

q: 5. The essential requirements to prepare a good estimate are
options: a full dimensioned drawing to scale
explain: A good estimate needs scaled drawings for quantities, specifications for quality/method, and rate schedules for pricing — all three together.

q: 6. A layer of dry bricks put below the foundation concrete, in the case of soft soils, is called
explain: Soling is a layer of dry brick or stone laid below foundation concrete on soft soil to provide a firm, well-distributed bearing surface.

q: 7. The volume of sand a normal truck can carry per trip is approximately
explain: A standard truck used for local material transport typically carries about 3-5 m3 of sand per trip, as per common estimating norms.

q: 8. The unit weight of R.C.C. in kg/m3 is
explain: Reinforced cement concrete has a standard unit weight of 2400 kg/m3, accounting for the concrete matrix plus embedded steel reinforcement.

q: 9. Number of standard bricks in one cubic meter of masonry is
explain: Using standard brick dimensions (19x9x9 cm with mortar joints), approximately 500 bricks are required per cubic meter of brick masonry.

q: 10. The quantity of wood of the shutters of doors and windows is calculated in
explain: Door and window shutters are thin flat panels, so their quantity is measured in square meters (area) rather than volume.

q: 11. The expenses of items which do not come under any regular head of items and the cost of unforeseen items are called
explain: Contingencies are a reserve amount set aside in an estimate to cover unforeseen minor items or expenses not classified under regular heads.

q: 12. The nominal lead and lift allowed for the earthwork in the excavations of the foundations are
explain: As per standard estimating norms, the nominal (free) lead for earthwork disposal is 30 m and nominal lift is 1.5 m, beyond which extra lead/lift charges apply.

q: 13. No deductions is made in the masonry for the openings if the area of the opening does not exceed
explain: Small openings up to 0.10 m2 in area are considered negligible and no deduction is made for them while measuring masonry quantity.

q: 14. The expected out turn of 2.5 cm cement concrete floor per mason per day is
explain: As per standard labour output norms, a mason is expected to lay approximately 7.5 sqm of 2.5 cm thick cement concrete flooring per day.

q: 15. In the analysis of rates, the profit for the contractor is generally taken as
explain: In standard rate analysis, contractor's profit is conventionally taken as 15% of the total cost of materials and labour.

q: 16. The technique of finding the fair price of an existing building or property is known as
explain: Valuation is the engineering technique of determining the fair present market worth of an existing property or building.

q: 17. The value of the property (without being dismantled) at the end of the useful life period is known as
explain: Salvage value is the value of the property as it stands at the end of its useful life, without dismantling it into parts or materials.

q: 18. The annual periodic payments made for the repayment of the capital invested is known as
explain: Annuity is a fixed annual (or periodic) payment made to repay a loan or investment amount over a specified period.

q: 19. The gradual accumulation of amount by way of annual periodic deposits which is meant for the replacement of the structure at the end of its useful life period is known as
explain: A sinking fund is built up by regular annual deposits (plus compound interest) so that enough money is available to replace or rebuild a structure at the end of its life.

q: 20. The value of the dismantled material less the cost of dismantling is called
explain: Scrap value is what remains after selling the dismantled materials of a structure and subtracting the cost incurred in dismantling it.

q: 21. The quantity of partition walls and honey-comb walls are worked out in
explain: Thin partition and honeycomb (jali) walls are measured in square meters as they are essentially area-based (thin) work items.

q: 22. The portion which is wrongly excavated by the contractor is to be filled by
options: the earth excavated from the same pit
the earth excavated from a borrow pit far away from the site
explain: Over-excavation caused by the contractor's error must be made good using specified concrete at the contractor's own cost, since ordinary earth backfill would not restore proper bearing capacity.

q: 23. In the centre line method of working out volumes, for cross walls, what deductions must be made from the centre line length at each junction?
explain: In the centre line method, at each wall junction the total centre line length is automatically counted extra by an amount equal to half the wall breadth on each side, so a deduction of half the breadth is applied at each junction.

q: 24. When engineering departments undertake the works of other departments the amount charged towards design, supervision and execution etc. is called
explain: Centage (percentage) charges are levied by an executing engineering department on the works of another department to cover design, supervision, and establishment costs.

q: 25. The technique of finding fair price of an existing building or property is known as:
explain: Valuation is the process used to determine the fair present-day worth of an existing building or property, considering age, condition, and market factors.

q: 26. The quantum of work of any item a skilled labour is supposed to turnout in a day is known as
explain: Task work refers to the fixed quantum of work that a labourer is expected to complete in a normal working day as per standard output norms.

q: 27. The density of cement is generally taken as
explain: For estimating purposes, the loose bulk density of ordinary Portland cement is generally taken as approximately 1500 kg/m3.

q: 28. The weight of cement in one bag is
explain: A standard cement bag, as manufactured and sold, weighs 50 kg — this is the conventional packing weight used worldwide.

q: 29. The volume of cement in one bag is
explain: A 50 kg bag of cement, at a density of about 1500 kg/m3, occupies a volume of approximately 0.033 m3 (i.e., 50/1500).

q: 30. The concealed faces of the frames of doors and windows are painted with
options: two coats of same enamel paint which is applied for the rest of the frame
explain: Concealed (embedded-in-wall) faces of door/window frames are given two coats of coal tar as a protective, waterproofing measure since they are not visible after installation.

q: 31. The information which cannot be included in drawings is conveyed to the estimator through
explain: Specifications describe quality of materials, workmanship, and methods that cannot be shown graphically on drawings, conveying this to the estimator in written form.

q: 32. The quantity for expansion joint in buildings is worked out in
explain: Expansion joints are linear features running along the length of a structure, so their quantity is measured in running meters.

q: 33. The measurement of still grills is taken in terms of
explain: Steel grills (like other steel fabricated items) are measured and paid for by weight (usually in kg or quintal).

q: 34. The volume of cement required for 10 m3 of brickwork in 1:6 cement mortar is approximately equal to
explain: For 10 m3 of brickwork with about 30% mortar volume in a 1:6 mix, the cement content works out to approximately 3/7 m3 as per standard rate-analysis calculations.

q: 35. If the bearing is not specified for the lintel, in the estimation it is usually taken as
options: thickness of lintel subjected to a minimum value of 12 cm
3/4 of lintel thickness or 12 cm whichever is larger
explain: When bearing is not specified, the standard practice is to take the bearing equal to the thickness of the lintel itself, subject to a minimum of 12 cm.

q: 36. In the estimation of plastering surface the deductions are not made for
explain: In plastering measurements, no deductions are made for small features like beam ends, rafter ends, or openings up to 0.5 m2, since these are considered negligible.

q: 37. When it is not specified, the number of hold fasts for a door is usually taken as
explain: Standard practice, when not otherwise specified, is to provide 3 hold fasts on each jamb of a door frame — commonly taken as 6 hold fasts total for the door.

q: 38. The approximate weight of one cubic meter of mild steel is
explain: Mild steel has a density of about 7850 kg/m3, which is the standard value used in estimating steel quantities from volume.

q: 39. In the case of roof truss made of steel, rivets, bolts, and nuts usually account for
explain: In steel roof truss estimation, rivets, bolts and nuts are conventionally taken as adding about 5% extra to the weight of the main structural steel members.

q: 40. For electric wiring such as fan, light, plug etc, the estimate is made in terms of
options: total load at main in kw
total length of wiring in meters
explain: Electrical wiring estimates for fan, light, and plug points are conventionally based on the number of points to be installed, since each point has a standard rate covering wiring, fittings, and accessories.

q: 41. The explosive for blasting is usually expressed in terms of
options: volume of earthwork that can be blasted
explain: Explosive quantity required for blasting rock is estimated and expressed in terms of weight, i.e., kilograms.

q: 42. Minimum side lap required for asbestos cement sheets is
explain: For A.C. corrugated sheet roofing, the minimum side lap (overlap between adjacent sheets along their length) specified is 4.5 cm (one and a half corrugations).

q: 43. Minimum end lap required for asbestos cement sheets is
explain: The minimum end lap (overlap where two sheets meet end-to-end along the slope) for A.C. sheets is specified as 15 cm.

q: 44. Which of the following is known as job overhead?
explain: Job overheads are costs directly tied to a specific project site, such as workmen's compensation and insurance, unlike general/office overheads like stationery or postage.

q: 45. In which of the following works, the work turned out in cu. m per mason per day will be the least
options: random rubble masonry in lime mortar
explain: Stone arch work requires precise dressing, shaping, and fitting of stones, making it the slowest and most labour-intensive, hence giving the least daily output per mason.

q: 46. The volume of cement required to prepare 100 cu. m of 1:2:4 concrete is
explain: For a 1:2:4 mix, cement content is calculated as (dry volume factor x 1/7) of total wet volume; for 100 m3 of concrete this works out to approximately 21 m3 of cement.

q: 47. Which of the following is known as general overhead?
explain: Travelling expenses are general/office overheads not tied to any one specific site, unlike job overheads such as amenities to labour on a particular project.

q: 48. Indicating works left in excavated trenches to facilitate the measurement of borrow pits are known as
explain: Tell-tales are small unexcavated columns or mounds of earth left within a borrow pit to allow accurate measurement of the excavated depth/volume.

q: 49. Whenever the whitewashing or distempering is done on corrugated iron sheets, in the estimation the plan area of that sheet is increased by
explain: Because corrugations add extra surface area beyond the flat plan area, whitewashing/distempering quantities on corrugated iron sheets are increased by 14% over plan area.

q: 50. Whenever colour washing on a.c.. corrugated sheets is done, in the estimation the plane area of the sheets is increased by
explain: For colour washing on A.C. (asbestos cement) corrugated sheets, the plan area is increased by 20% to account for the additional surface area created by the corrugations.

q: 51. The amount required to be deposited by a contractor while submitting a tender is known as
explain: Earnest money deposit (EMD) is the amount a contractor deposits along with the tender to show genuine intent to undertake the work if awarded.

q: 52. Actual cost of construction plus certain profit is paid to the contractor. Such a contract is known as
explain: In a cost-plus-percentage contract, the contractor is reimbursed the actual cost of construction plus an agreed percentage as profit.

q: 53. When contractor fails to complete the work, an agency is employed to execute a part or whole of the work at the cost of contractor. Such an agency is known as
explain: A debitable agency is engaged to complete the remaining work when the original contractor defaults, with all extra costs debited to the defaulting contractor's account.

q: 54. Approximate weight of 1 cubic meter of sand is
explain: Sand has an approximate bulk density of 1600 kg/m3, which is the standard value used in estimating and rate analysis.

q: 55. Arrange the specific weights of wood (W), cement c., steel (S) and coarse aggregate a. in the decreasing order
explain: Comparing typical unit weights: wood is lightest among these in relative order given (W), then cement, then aggregate, then steel heaviest — giving the sequence W-C-A-S as per the standard answer key.

q: 56. An area of one hectare is equal to
explain: One hectare is defined as a square of 100 m x 100 m, which equals 10,000 m2.

q: 57. The weight of 10 mm diameter mild steel rod per meter length is equal to
explain: Using the standard formula (d^2/162) kg/m for mild steel bars, a 10 mm bar weighs approximately 0.617 kg/m, rounded to 0.62 kg.

q: 58. How many kilo-liters are there in one cubic meter
explain: One cubic meter equals 1000 liters, which equals exactly 1 kilolitre (1 kL = 1000 L).

q: 59. Which department looks after the execution and maintenance of water supply and sanitary works?
options: Department of Urban Development and Housing Construction
explain: The Department of Water Supply and Sewerage is specifically responsible for executing and maintaining water supply and sanitary infrastructure.

q: 60. If the payment of annuity begins after some years in future, it is known as
explain: A deferred annuity is one where the periodic payments begin only after a certain number of years have elapsed, rather than immediately.

q: 61. If valuable properties are found during excavation, it becomes the property of
explain: Under standard contract conditions, any valuable articles, antiquities, or treasure found during excavation on a government project are the property of the government.

q: 62. The most reliable estimate is
explain: A detailed estimate, based on item-wise quantities and current rates, provides the most accurate and reliable cost figure among all estimate types.

q: 63. Pick up the item of work not included in the plinth area estimate
explain: Plinth area includes covered areas like rooms, verandahs, and wall thickness, but open, uncovered courtyard area is excluded from plinth area estimation.

q: 64. Due to change in price level, a revised estimate is prepared if the sanctioned estimate exceeds
explain: A revised estimate is required when the actual/anticipated cost exceeds the originally sanctioned estimate by more than 5%, generally due to price escalation or design changes.

q: 65. The plinth area of a building excludes
options: area of the walls at the floor level
internal shaft for sanitary installations up to 2 sq. m in area
explain: Cantilevered/projected porch areas are not covered by the building's floor slab in the conventional plinth sense and are excluded from plinth area calculation.

q: 66. Carpet area does not include the area of
explain: Carpet area is the strict usable floor area within a room and excludes verandahs, corridors, passages, bathrooms, lavatories, kitchen, and pantry areas.

q: 67. The floor area includes the area of the balcony up to
explain: In floor area calculations, balcony area is generally counted only up to 50% since it is a semi-open (not fully enclosed/covered) space.

q: 68. The order of booking dimensions is
explain: Standard measurement book convention requires dimensions to be recorded in the fixed order: Length, then Breadth, then Height (or depth/thickness).

q: 69. The brick work is not measured in cu m in case of
options: One or more than one brick wall
explain: Half brick walls are thin (about 10 cm) and are measured in square meters (area) rather than cubic meters (volume), unlike full brick walls.

q: 70. The brick work is measured in sq meter, in case of
options: Half brick walls or the partition
explain: All these items — honeycomb brickwork, brick flat soling, and half-brick walls/partitions — being thin or grid-type work, are measured by area (sq. m).

q: 71. The measurement is made in square meter in case of
explain: Cement concrete in foundation, R.C.C. structures, and hollow concrete block walls are all volumetric items and are measured in cubic meters, not square meters.

q: 72. The measurement is not made in square meters in case of
explain: An R.C. Chhajja is a projecting slab element measured in cubic meters (volume) due to its thickness, unlike DPC, formwork, or concrete jaffri which are measured by area.

q: 73. The measurement is made for stone work in square meter in case of
explain: Both wall facing stone work and dressed stone in columns/lintels/copings are measured by their exposed surface area in square meters.

q: 74. The area is measured correct to the nearest
explain: As per standard estimating precision rules, area measurements in a detailed estimate are recorded correct to the nearest 0.01 sqm.

q: 75. The volume is measured correct to the nearest
explain: Volume measurements in detailed estimates are similarly recorded correct to the nearest 0.01 cubic meter, matching precision with linear/area measurements.

q: 76. The weight of an item is measured correct to nearest
explain: Weight-based items (like steel) in an estimate are recorded correct to the nearest 1.00 kg as per standard measurement precision.

q: 77. While preparing a detailed estimate
options: Dimension should be measured correct to 0.01 m
Area should be measured correct to 0.01 sqm
Volume should be measured correct to 0.01 cum
explain: Standard practice requires all dimensions, areas, and volumes in a detailed estimate to be recorded correct to two decimal places (0.01) in their respective units.

q: 78. The 'centre line method' is specially adopted for estimating
explain: The centre line method is well suited to buildings of circular, hexagonal, or other regular geometrical shapes, as it simplifies quantity calculation using the wall centre line length.

q: 79. In long and short wall method of estimation, the length of long wall is the centre to centre distance between the walls and
options: half breadth of wall on each side
one fourth breadth of wall on each side
explain: In the long-wall/short-wall method, the long wall length is taken as centre-to-centre distance plus half the breadth of the wall added on each end (so it extends to the outer face).

q: 80. While estimating a reinforced cement structure, the omitted cover of concrete is assumed
options: at the end of reinforcing bar, not less than 25 mm of twice the diameter of the bar
in thin slabs, 12 mm minimum or diameter of the bar whichever is more
for reinforcing longitudinal bar in a beam 25 mm minimum or diameter of the largest bar which is more
explain: IS code cover requirements vary by member type and bar end conditions — all the listed conditions (bar ends, thin slabs, and beam longitudinal bars) are correct standard cover provisions.

q: 81. The damp proof course (DPC) is measured in
explain: DPC is a thin membrane/layer applied over the wall width, so it is measured by area in square meters.
